source: Isermann (2004/2005) Model-based fault detection and diagnosis: status and applications
finding: Classical supervision is limit or trend checking of single signals. It is simple and reliable but reacts only after a large or long-lasting change and gives no diagnosis. Model-based methods use input and output signals and a dynamic model to compute features, then symptoms by change detection, then a diagnosis.
numbers: Four stated requirements: early detection of small abrupt or incipient faults; diagnosis of actuator, component and sensor faults; detection in closed loops; supervision in transient states.
limits: IFAC conference version, not the 2005 Annual Reviews text. Gives the framework, little quantitative comparison.
agent_relevance: A cheap threshold check first, then a model of expected behaviour, then symptoms, then diagnosis. Detection and diagnosis are separate steps.

source: Isermann (2004/2005) Model-based fault detection and diagnosis: status and applications
finding: Three residual-generation families. Parameter estimation suits multiplicative faults and needs input excitation. State and output observers need known parameters and model additive faults at input and output. Parity equations run a fixed model beside the process and form an output error.
numbers: Applications shown: electric actuator, passenger car lateral dynamics, combustion engine. Parameter estimates identify parametric faults; parity residuals identify additive sensor offsets; cross couplings exist.
quote: A fault is defined as an unpermitted deviation of at least one characteristic property of a variable from an acceptable behaviour.
limits: All three need a good process model; faults the model cannot represent give misleading residuals.
agent_relevance: Residual = observed minus expected from a model. For the agent: compare an attempt's output with a prediction and treat the gap as the symptom.

source: Isermann (2004/2005) Model-based fault detection and diagnosis: status and applications
finding: Diagnosis step: symptoms (analytical and heuristic) are classified by statistical or geometric classifiers or neural nets, or reasoned over with fault trees (cause to symptom) and event trees (symptom to cause, forward chaining).
limits: Qualitative description only.
agent_relevance: Separates a detection signal from a diagnostic inference over a causal structure.

source: Ahang et al. (2024) Intelligent condition monitoring of industrial plants: an overview of methodologies and uncertainty management strategies
finding: Survey of deep learning fault detection and diagnosis on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP). It traces the lineage from limit checks and Isermann's model-based work to PCA, PLS, dynamic PCA, CVA, then RNN, CNN and autoencoders. TEP is the most used benchmark.
numbers: Averages cited from other papers: an RNN 92.5% over all faults but cannot detect fault 15; LSTM 95%; GRU 95.9% (Mirzaei 2022); a CNN 96.2% when faults 3, 9, 15 are excluded.
limits: Numbers are second-hand from cited papers with different protocols; not comparable.
agent_relevance: Headline accuracies often hide dropped hard faults. Check which cases a score leaves out.

source: Downs and Vogel (1993) Tennessee Eastman Process, as described in Ahang et al. (2024) and FaultExplainer (2024)
finding: The TEP is a simulated chemical plant with five units (reactor, condenser, separator, compressor, stripper), eight components A to H, closed-loop control and 21 preprogrammed faults. It became the standard testbed for fault detection research.
numbers: 41 measured and 12 manipulated variables (52 or 53 in use); 21 faults, 15 with known root cause. Fault modes include step, random variation, slow drift, sticking.
limits: Original paper not opened; facts taken from papers that describe it. It is a simulation.
agent_relevance: A rare shared benchmark with known ground-truth causes. Useful for testing an LLM diagnostic agent, but a single simulator.

source: Peng et al. (2017) Neural component analysis for fault detection
finding: Protocol: PCA, kernel PCA, autoencoder and NCA monitored with T2 and SPE (squared prediction error) statistics, control limit by kernel density estimate, alpha 0.01. 500 normal training samples; 960 test samples per fault with the fault starting at sample 161; 52 variables. A case counts only if missed detection is under 50% and false alarm under 5%.
numbers: NCA best in 11 of 21 faults, kernel PCA 7, autoencoder 5, PCA 4.
limits: Single simulator run per fault; no confidence intervals in the text read.
agent_relevance: Shows the standard recipe: normal-only training, a statistic, a limit set by false alarm rate.

source: Peng et al. (2017) Neural component analysis for fault detection
finding: Faults 3, 9 and 15 are essentially undetectable by every method in this table with false alarm under 5%.
numbers: T2 missed rate: fault 3 PCA 92.0, KPCA 93.8, AE 96.4, NCA 98.4 percent. Fault 9: 96.4, 94.1, 96.0, 94.0. Fault 15: 95.1, 94.1, 94.3, 97.5. PCA SPE gives 71.9, 76.9, 74.4 missed but with false alarms of 30.0, 23.8, 16.9 percent.
limits: False alarms are measured over the first 160 samples only, so one false alarm is 0.63%.
agent_relevance: A detector that looks good on average can be blind to a whole fault class. The agent should know which fault types its checks cannot see.

source: Peng et al. (2017) Neural component analysis for fault detection
finding: A low miss rate can be bought with false alarms. PCA's SPE gives the lowest missed rates on many faults at false alarm rates of 10 to 31 percent, so it fails the 5% rule.
numbers: PCA SPE: fault 1 miss 0.13% at FAR 20.6%; fault 2 0.75% at 18.1%; fault 4 0.00% at 24.4%; fault 7 0.00% at 16.3%. NCA SPE on fault 4: miss 5.75% at FAR 0.63%. Autoencoder SPE on fault 7: miss 30.1% vs KPCA 2.0% and NCA 0.00%.
limits: Authors blame PCA's linear residual subspace for the bad limit and autoencoder overfitting for the fault 7 failure; neither tested separately.
agent_relevance: Detection trades misses against false alarms. G1 (doubt only on a signal) needs a signal with a known false-alarm rate.

source: On the optimality of Kalman filter for fault detection (2023)
finding: Kalman-filter residuals are optimal for state estimation, but that does not make them optimal for fault detection. For a low-pass fault (step, drift) the best residual filter is a frequency selector; the Kalman residual is an all-pass whitening filter and is worse unless the fault is broadband.
numbers: Monte Carlo, 5000 runs per case: step fault amplitude 30; drift amplitude 60; sine amplitude 0.6 at frequency 0.4. Optimal filter plus output error gave the best detection rate; the pure Kalman residual gave a large peak then a sharp drop.
limits: Authors not recorded. Stationary linear Gaussian theory; assumes the fault is low-pass.
agent_relevance: Residual designs must match the fault signature. An optimal estimator is not automatically an optimal detector.

source: On the optimality of Kalman filter for fault detection (2023)
finding: Check on TEP (21 documented faults, residuals from identified models): a filter-bank scheme (OEFB) beats Kalman residuals on hard faults 3, 9, 15.
numbers: Detection rate percent, faults 3 / 9 / 15: SAP 6.4 / 0.9 / 29.5; output error 18.6 / 8.4 / 21.1; OEFB 93.9 / 84.4 / 91.5; Kalman s=0 26.0 / 44.0 / 56.3; s=10 73.3 / 72.8 / 84.4; s=20 91.1 / 74.6 / 86.9. Raising s lifts mean detection and mean false alarm together.
limits: Model-based protocol differs from the PCA papers, so not comparable. Table columns read from a text extract.
agent_relevance: Faults 3, 9, 15 are detectable with the right filter, so the 'impossible' label in PCA papers is a method limit.

source: Gao, Wang, Chen (2024) Autoencoder-assisted Feature Ensemble Net for incipient faults
finding: Authors say deep networks, even with prior fault information, have not detected TEP faults 3, 9, 15. Plain PCA on their protocol catches almost none.
numbers: PCA detection rate: fault 3 5.70%, fault 9 7.70%, fault 15 3.05%; normal-data false alarm 1.70%. Protocol: 4000 normal training samples; test 4000 samples, 2000 normal then 2000 faulty; confidence 0.99; window 150.
limits: The paper calls the rate FDR and in two places 'False Discovery Rates'; read as detection rate.
agent_relevance: Incipient faults are where single-statistic checks fail. Baseline numbers to beat.

source: Gao, Wang, Chen (2024) Autoencoder-assisted Feature Ensemble Net for incipient faults
finding: Feature ensemble: slide a window, build several base detectors (PCA, DPCA, three Mahalanobis distances), then transform the features again in layers. Replacing PCA with an autoencoder in the transform layers raises detection on hard faults.
numbers: FENet average FDR 79.05% (0 layers), 92.35% (1), 95.38% (2). AE-FENet 2 layers average 98.66%; faults 3, 9, 15 at 97.55%, 97.55%, 96.05%. FENet 2 layers: fault 3 91.50, fault 9 94.25, fault 15 80.80. Sparse AE-FENet average 94.57%.
limits: Authors' own method, one protocol, no independent replication found. Long fault segment (2000 samples) makes detection easier than short-test protocols.
agent_relevance: Ensembling different views then re-ensembling helps incipient faults. Compare G4: diversity matters, not just more samples.

source: Pozdnyakov et al. (2024) Adversarial attacks and defenses in fault detection and diagnosis: a benchmark on the Tennessee Eastman Process
finding: Three neural diagnosers (MLP, GRU, TCN) reach similar clean accuracy on TEP and all collapse under six adversarial attacks. A black-box attacker needs only input and output data.
numbers: Clean accuracy: MLP 0.8873 +- 0.0002 (3,452,949 parameters); GRU 0.9067 +- 0.0041 (204,565); TCN 0.8985 +- 0.0097 (151,935). Window 32. Attack strength eps: 20 values from 0 to 0.3 in steps of 0.015.
quote: All three neural network architectures have proven to be highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks and require protection methods.
limits: Perturbation in standardised units; a real attacker needs access to the data link. Defence settings tuned only on TCN.
agent_relevance: Learned diagnosers are brittle to small input changes. A scaffold that relies on a fixed learned detector inherits this.

source: Pozdnyakov et al. (2024) Adversarial attacks and defenses in fault detection and diagnosis: a benchmark on the Tennessee Eastman Process
finding: Five defences tested. Adversarial training with PGD samples and an autoencoder front end are the only broadly effective ones, but both cost clean accuracy. Training against one eps does not transfer to others. Quantisation (n=5 levels) combined with adversarial training was proposed as a trade-off.
numbers: Clean-data accuracy drops noticeably for the autoencoder defence (exact values in their Tables 2 to 5, not extracted).
limits: Exact defended accuracies not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Robustness checks cost accuracy; validate on perturbed and held-out inputs (G3).

source: FaultExplainer: leveraging large language models for interpretable fault detection and diagnosis (2024)
finding: A PCA monitor detects a fault on TEP, takes the six features that deviate most, and feeds them with a process description to an LLM, which reports likely root causes. Two prompts: a known list of 15 root causes (top three), and open reasoning.
numbers: Only 11 of the 21 faults are detected by PCA. With the 15-cause list: GPT-4o correct on 7 of 11, o1-preview 9 of 11; neither identifies fault 5 (condenser cooling water step) or fault 10 (C feed temperature random variation). Aliases (1/8, 3/9, 5/15) counted correct.
limits: Authors not recorded. Tiny sample (11 faults), one run per model, no repeat variance, judged by the authors.
agent_relevance: Detector plus LLM explainer is the same shape as our design: code decides when to look, the model explains. Diagnosis accuracy depends on the detector's feature choice.

source: FaultExplainer: leveraging large language models for interpretable fault detection and diagnosis (2024)
finding: Open reasoning (no list) is weaker on slow-drift and random-variation faults. Both models give coherent but wrong causal stories when the selected features are indirect, and some explanations contain hallucinated claims.
numbers: Open prompt: both models found a correct or related cause in 8 of 11 detected faults; neither for faults 10 and 13 (reaction kinetics slow drift). o1-preview gave more detailed, causally ordered explanations than GPT-4o.
limits: Plausibility of an explanation did not track correctness: o1-preview's wrong fault 10 answer was coherent.
agent_relevance: Fluent explanation is not evidence. Require a check against held-out signals before accepting a root cause (G2, G3).

source: Golyadkin et al. (2023) SensorSCAN: self-supervised learning and deep clustering for fault diagnosis in chemical processes
finding: Unsupervised fault detection and diagnosis by self-supervised features and clustering, tested on two TEP datasets (Rieth and Ricker versions). It gains over prior unsupervised methods at a fixed false positive rate.
numbers: +0.2 to +0.3 true positive rate at fixed false positive rate versus existing approaches; FPR threshold 0.05; more clusters than faults does not drop performance much; a model fine-tuned on a small labelled fraction nearly reaches a fully supervised state of the art.
limits: Abstract, method and setup read; full per-fault tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Labels are not needed to find that something changed; labels are needed only to name it.

source: Agarwal et al. (2020) Hierarchical deep recurrent neural network based method for fault detection and diagnosis
finding: Statistical monitors miss incipient faults. Authors group similar faults into a hierarchy (level one non-incipient, level two incipient) and inject a pseudo-random binary signal to expose incipient faults.
numbers: On 17 non-incipient faults, average detection: PCA T2 61.77%, PCA SPE 74.72%, DPCA 72.35%, ICA 87.29%. Level one: 7382 training and 17,442 test samples; level two: 1796 training and 4196 test samples, horizon 150.
limits: Authors' own method; hierarchical average accuracy not extracted. Probing signal needs the ability to act on the plant.
agent_relevance: Active probing (inject a test signal and watch the response) exposes faults passive monitoring cannot see. It parallels testing a hypothesis by experiment.

source: Aryal, Modekwe, Lu (2026) Multi-level temporal graph networks with local-global fusion for industrial fault diagnosis
finding: A correlation graph over sensors, an LSTM encoder, graph convolution and multi-level pooling beat five baselines on 20 TEP fault classes with a 100-sample sliding window (stride 1).
numbers: Average FDR and F1 96.6%, precision 96.7%. Best deep baseline LSTM-CNN 94.1% FDR; an ANN baseline 80.8% FDR and 81.8% F1. Fault 3 F1: GraphSAGE 82.0% to 97.0%.
limits: Classification of labelled faults, not detection from normal-only data; supervised. Authors' own method, preprint.
agent_relevance: Supervised classifiers reach about 97% on faults that unsupervised statistics miss: the labels carry the information, so this is not a like-for-like result.

source: Peng, Zhao, Hu (2021) Second-order component analysis for fault detection
finding: Abstract only: a second-order autoencoder with orthogonal constraints, optimised on a Stiefel manifold, beats PCA, kernel PCA and autoencoder on TEP in missed detection and false alarm rate.
limits: Only the abstract and start of the introduction were read. No numbers.
agent_relevance: Same research line as NCA; continued claims of improvement over PCA.

source: Kovalenko, Pozdnyakov, Makarov (2022) Graph neural networks with trainable adjacency matrices for fault diagnosis on multivariate sensor data
finding: Abstract only: learns the sensor graph during training and outperforms recurrent nets on TEP fault diagnosis.
limits: Only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Sensor dependency structure is learnable without prior knowledge.

source: Gravanis et al. (2026) Explainability for fault detection system in chemical processes
finding: Abstract only: Integrated Gradients and SHAP explain an LSTM fault classifier on TEP; they mostly name the same features, and SHAP sometimes is closer to the root cause.
limits: Only the abstract was read. No numbers.
agent_relevance: Feature attribution can point at the subsystem; it is a hint, not proof of cause.

source: Liang and Sina (2026) LLM as client coordinating diagnostic tools on TEP (from a search summary)
finding: Search summary: an LLM coordinates diagnostic tools through a unified protocol; the paper argues an ensemble of multi-scale CNNs gives more reliable output for the LLM.
numbers: One ensemble reported at 68.04% accuracy (from the search summary).
limits: Not opened; figures unverified.
agent_relevance: Tool-using LLM over detectors matches our design; verify before citing.

source: Huang et al. (2024) pretrained LLMs choose fault-relevant channels with data-driven anomaly detection (from a search summary)
finding: Search summary: an LLM picks relevant channels, combined with anomaly detection; the authors claim very high root-cause accuracy on TEP.
numbers: No figure available.
limits: Not opened; claim unverified.
agent_relevance: Another detector plus LLM hybrid; needs the paper for numbers.

source: Synthesis across a05-a19: TEP protocols differ between papers
finding: TEP numbers are not comparable between papers. Test length (960 vs 4000 samples), fault onset, window size (32, 100, 150), false alarm limit and whether faults 3, 9, 15 are dropped all differ.
numbers: NCA: 960 test samples, fault at sample 161. AE-FENet: 2000 normal and 2000 faulty. Adversarial benchmark: window 32. LGF-MLTG: window 100. Supervised classifiers reach 94 to 98% while PCA gets 3 to 8% on faults 3, 9, 15 in the AE-FENet protocol.
limits: Our reading of the papers above, not a published meta-analysis. No formal replication of any of these results was found in this pass.
agent_relevance: Do not quote one TEP accuracy as a general result; keep the protocol with the number.

source: Synthesis across a05-a14: detection, localisation and diagnosis are separate problems
finding: Three separate problems: detect that something changed (set by false alarm rate), find which variables moved (contribution analysis), and name the cause (needs a causal model or labels). LLM work so far addresses the last step, on top of a fixed detector.
numbers: FaultExplainer: 11 of 21 faults detected by PCA; 7 or 9 of 11 diagnosed with a cause list; 8 of 11 without one.
limits: Our synthesis.
agent_relevance: Agent design: code runs the detector, the model explains one failing signal, and a check on held-out data confirms.
